problem: Demand-driven navigation (DDN, MO-DDN) handles a single need at a time, so it cannot handle long-horizon instructions with several sub-demands and explicit task preferences. Existing long-horizon or memory-based methods target object-goal navigation, and calling an LLM at every step is too slow.
motivation: Real users have a series of needs (clean, rest, eat), each with a personal preference, and the agent must decompose them, track completion and keep a spatial memory over long trajectories. The paper is driven by the need to balance LLM reasoning depth against cost, and to recover from collisions and loops in simulation.
key_idea: Introduce the TP-MDDN benchmark and solve it with a training-free LLM/MLLM decision system (BreakLLM, LocateLLM, StatusMLLM) on a lightweight accumulated semantic map (MASMap), executed by a slow/fast dual-tempo action generator with adaptive error correction.
insight: Task-status tracking and error correction matter for long-horizon success: removing StatusMLLM drops SR from 32.00 to 27.33, and removing block correction or beyond-boundary correction drops SR to 28.00 and 27.33. The reasoning LLM's scale matters (Qwen2.5-VL-72B SR 32.00 vs 7B 19.33 vs GPT-4o 28.67), as does the segmenter (RAM-Grounded-SAM 32.00 vs GLEE 21.33). Dual-tempo execution keeps time at 6.82 min per instruction versus 88.90 min for InstructNav.
method: TP-MDDN benchmark: ProcTHOR test scenes (68 rooms), 200 long-horizon instructions with 3 subtasks each, generated by DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o and manually checked; a subtask succeeds if the agent is within 1.5 m of a matching object.

MASMap: Ram-Grounded-SAM on panoramic RGB, with depth lifted to per-object 3D point clouds. Clouds are merged by overlap thresholds (new object if max os<0.25, merge if os and ros>0.8). Object centers and bboxes then go into a 2D semantic map with IoU plus Hungarian matching, and the 3D points are discarded to save memory.
BreakLLM: decomposes the instruction into a subtask list and initializes a status list to False.

LocateLLM: takes the instruction, subtasks, status, target memory (target, xy, feedback type) and object memory, and picks the next target object/position. When consecutive failures reach 2, an extra prompt forbids that object/position.
StatusMLLM: triggered when the fast-tempo policy outputs Done; from the current image, target memory and previous status it judges which subtask was completed and updates the status list.

Dual-Tempo action generator: the slow tempo runs LocateLLM, builds an affordance map (obstacle plus target-distance affordance, as in InstructNav), plans with A*, and samples waypoints into discrete actions. The fast tempo runs the pretrained DDN policy near targets with 6 low-level actions.

Adaptive Error Corrector: on predicted collisions or out-of-bounds moves it recomputes the affordance map and re-plans, using a finer waypoint interval n_block for the initial segment and the standard n_waypoint afterwards.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-72B (frozen) as LLM/MLLM, Ram-Grounded-SAM for segmentation, pretrained DDN policy for fast control
setting.action_space: discrete: MoveAhead 0.25 m, Rotate 30°, LookUp/LookDown, Done; waypoints via A*
setting.privileged: none stated (agent pose used for mapping)

numbers.eval_set_note: 50 tasks per method, averaged over 3 runs (from the 200 generated instructions)
numbers.extra: max 50 steps, success radius 1.5 m; the table marks zero-shot as ✗ because of the pretrained DDN policy
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Comparison with state-of-the-art methods on the TP-MDDN benchmark, AWM-Nav row

numbers_note: Own benchmark; the split is not named in the paper, so 'test' is assumed (ProcTHOR test set). Execution time: 6.82 min per instruction for AWM-Nav.
results: AWM-Nav reaches SR 32.00 and ISR 62.89 on TP-MDDN, twice the SR of DDN and InstructNav (both 16.00); MO-DDN gets 13.33. It is much faster than InstructNav (6.82 vs 88.90 min per instruction) but slower than DDN (1.74 min).
limitations: Involuntary mode switching in the dual-tempo framework and over-reliance on pretrained LLMs, which can misjudge instructions.
Evaluated on only 50 tasks per method in a single simulator with 3-subtask instructions; MO-DDN is a reimplementation because its code is not public.
